content: Flavonoids are a class of secondary metabolites found in plants. According to the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) nomenclature, flavonoids are categorized into three main groups based on their chemical structure: flavonoids (derived from 2-phenylchromen-4-one), isoflavonoids (derived from 3-phenylchromen-4-one), and neoflavonoids (derived from 4-phenylcoumarine). These compounds are widely recognized for their antioxidant properties, but their health benefits, particularly in cancer and cardiovascular disease prevention, are attributed to mechanisms beyond direct antioxidant activity. Flavonoids are also referred to as bioflavonoids, as they are of biological origin. Flavonoids are synthesized in plants through the phenylpropanoid metabolic pathway, which begins with the amino acid phenylalanine. This pathway produces 4-coumaroyl-CoA, which combines with malonyl-CoA to form chalcones, the precursors of flavonoids. Chalcones undergo ring closure to form the characteristic three-ring structure of flavones. Further enzymatic modifications along this pathway yield various flavonoid subtypes, including flavanones, dihydroflavonols, anthocyanins, flavonols, flavan-3-ols, and proanthocyanidins (tannins). Flavonoids serve multiple biological functions in plants, such as producing yellow, red, or blue pigmentation in flowers and providing protection against microbial and insect attacks. Their widespread distribution, structural diversity, and low toxicity compared to other plant compounds (e.g., alkaloids) make them a significant dietary component for humans and animals. Flavonoids have been described as nature's biological response modifiers due to their ability to influence the body's reactions to allergens, viruses, and carcinogens. They exhibit anti-allergic, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and anti-cancer activities. Their potential role in preventing cancers and cardiovascular diseases has garnered interest from consumers and food manufacturers. The health benefits of flavonoid-rich foods, such as fruits, vegetables, tea, and red wine, are often attributed to these compounds rather than to traditional nutrients or vitamins. Research conducted in 2007 at the Linus Pauling Institute revealed that flavonoids have minimal direct antioxidant activity within the human body. Unlike in vitro conditions, flavonoids are poorly absorbed (less than 5%) and are rapidly metabolized and excreted. The observed increase in blood antioxidant capacity after consuming flavonoid-rich foods is likely due to elevated uric acid levels resulting from flavonoid metabolism, rather than the flavonoids themselves. Flavonoids may also activate mechanisms that promote cancer cell death and inhibit tumor invasion. Importantly, only small amounts of flavonoids are needed to achieve these health benefits, and excessive supplementation offers no additional advantage and may pose risks. A study conducted at Children’s Hospital & Research Center Oakland, in collaboration with Heinrich Heine University, demonstrated that certain flavonoids, such as epicatechin, quercetin, and luteolin, can inhibit fluid secretion in the intestines, which is associated with diarrhea. This effect is achieved by targeting the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) chloride transport and inhibiting cAMP-stimulated chloride secretion. Quercetin, a flavonol, is one of the most biologically active flavonoids and is found in high concentrations in many medicinal plants. It exhibits significant anti-inflammatory activity by directly inhibiting the production and release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators. Quercetin also has potent antioxidant properties, enhances vitamin C activity, and demonstrates anti-cancer effects. It is commonly found in herbal products derived from hawthorn, which are used to treat acute symptoms of congestive heart failure. Epicatechin, a flavonoid found in cocoa and dark chocolate, improves blood flow and supports cardiovascular health. Cocoa contains high levels of epicatechin and has been shown to have greater antioxidant content than red wine or green tea in vitro. However, the antioxidant effects in vivo are minimal due to rapid excretion. Proanthocyanidins, another class of flavonoids, exhibit a wide range of pharmacological activities, including increasing intracellular vitamin C levels, reducing capillary permeability and fragility, scavenging free radicals, and protecting collagen from degradation. Dietary sources of flavonoids include citrus fruits, berries, onions, parsley, legumes, green tea, red wine, and dark chocolate (with at least 70% cocoa content). Citrus bioflavonoids, such as hesperidin, quercetin, rutin, and tangeritin, have antioxidant properties, enhance vitamin C levels, and improve capillary permeability and blood flow. They also share some anti-allergic and anti-inflammatory benefits with quercetin. Quercetin has been shown to inhibit reverse transcriptase, a key enzyme in retrovirus replication, though the clinical relevance of this effect remains unclear. Hydroxyethylrutosides (HER) are used to treat conditions such as capillary permeability, easy bruising, hemorrhoids, and varicose veins. Green tea flavonoids, particularly catechins (e.g., epicatechin, epigallocatechin gallate), are potent antioxidants thought to reduce the risk of cancer and heart disease. Unlike black or oolong tea, green tea is produced by steaming fresh leaves, which prevents oxidation and preserves catechins. Grape skins, used in wine production, are rich in flavonoids and other polyphenols. Red wine, fermented with grape skins, contains higher levels of flavonoids and resveratrol compared to white wine. Over 5,000 naturally occurring flavonoids have been identified and classified based on their chemical structure. Subgroups include flavones (e.g., luteolin, apigenin), flavonols (e.g., quercetin, kaempferol), flavanones (e.g., hesperetin, naringenin), isoflavones (e.g., genistein, daidzein), flavan-3-ols (e.g., catechins, epicatechins), and anthocyanidins (e.g., cyanidin, delphinidin). Recent research has also demonstrated the efficient production of flavonoids using genetically engineered microorganisms.
